claim: Across the entire sample, a family history of Alzheimer's disease is present in 22.76% of participants.

claim: The percentage of participants with family history of Alzheimer's disease increases with age.
source: Across the entire sample, a FH of AD is present in 22.76% with the overall percentage swelling with age (Figure 1D).

claim: Age was significantly associated with PAL performance (BAge = −0.20 word pairs, pAge <2e-16).

evidence: The manuscript reports statistical coefficients and p-values from the GLM analysis.

claim: Age was associated with a lowered PAL performance of two word-pairs per decade of life.
source: Age was associated with a lowered PAL performance of two word-pairs per decade of life (Figure 2).

claim: Women were associated with nearly a two word-pair higher PAL score compared to men.

claim: The disparity between women's and men's PAL scores markedly grew around the 5th decade of life.

evidence: The manuscript provides specific effect size estimates from PSM analysis.

source: In women and men, PSM revealed an approximate effect size of one-word pair higher performance across each level of Educational Attainment (e.g., Male 12y vs. 14y [ATT0.72 ± SD0.28], Female 12y vs. 14y=[ATT1.06 ± SD0.24]).

source: These data indicated that in FH +participants, there was an association of one and a third word pair lower PAL score per each ε4 allele.

claim: Having a first-degree relative diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease is associated with lower verbal learning and memory performance below the age of 65.
source: Overall, this study finds that having a first-degree relative diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease (FH) is associated with lower verbal learning and memory performance (i.e., paired-associates learning; PAL) below the age of 65.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: FH men showed a greater reduction in cognition compared to FH women.
source: Notably, FH men showed a greater reduction in cognition compared to FH women.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sex difference in FH effect.

claim: Women, regardless of FH, perform better on PAL compared to men.
source: This effect is not surprising since women, regardless of FH, perform better on PAL compared to men (Kaushanskaya et al., 2011), an effect replicated in this study.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation and replication in the current study.

claim: This is the first time the sex-effect for PAL has been demonstrated across the entire adult lifespan in a large cohort using the same test in a single study.
source: To that end, we demonstrate the sex-effect for PAL extends across the entire adult lifespan; indeed, the first time to the authors' knowledge that this has been demonstrated: 1) in a large cohort, 2) using the same test, and 3) in a single study.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly claims this is a novel demonstration.

claim: The 5th decade of life is the approximate age when women undergo menopause in developed countries.
source: The 5th decade of life is the approximate age when women undergo menopause in developed countries.
evidence: The manuscript states a fact about menopause timing.

claim: Menopause-related changes to women's hormonal milieu, either endogenously or via hormone treatment or gynecological surgery have been found to alter cognition during this period.
source: Menopause-related changes to women's hormonal milieu, either endogenously or via hormone treatment or gynecological surgery have been found to alter cognition during this period (discussed in Koebele and Bimonte-Nelson, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Education in women was associated with better PAL scores compared to men, at all except the highest reported level of educational attainment (i.e., 16 vs. 20 years of education), regardless of FH status.
source: Lastly, educational attainment was associated with milestone-dependent higher learning and memory performance. Regardless of FH status, education in women was associated with better PAL scores compared to men, at all except the highest reported level of educational attainment (i.e., 16 vs. 20 years of education).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sex difference in education effect.

claim: Higher levels of education are associated with delayed AD onset.
source: The effect of education on PAL scores is in line with observations in a clinical study demonstrating that higher levels of education are associated with delayed AD onset (Vemuri et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Diabetes modified the effect of FH on PAL.
source: In terms of health, lifestyle, and genetic factors, this study found that diabetes modified the effect of FH on PAL.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that diabetes modifies FH effect.

claim: In both women and men, diabetes and FH were associated with reduced PAL performance.
source: Specifically, in both women and men, diabetes and FH were associated with reduced PAL performance.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the combined effect of diabetes and FH.

claim: Diabetes has been linked to worse cognitive deficits in AD.
source: It is not surprising that diabetes exacerbates the effects of FH on cognition since diabetes has been linked to worse cognitive deficits in AD (Takeda and Morishita, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The presence of an APOE ε4 allele was associated with lower PAL performance in a dose-dependent-like manner in FH individuals.
source: As for genetic factors that modify FH, we supported our hypothesis whereby the presence of an APOE ε4 allele was associated with lower PAL performance in a dose-dependent-like manner in FH individuals.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the APOE ε4 effect in FH individuals.

claim: APOE genotype is an important genetic factor that influences memory.
source: These data suggest that APOE genotype is an important genetic factor that influences memory.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the APOE findings.

claim: A voxel-wise study in humans noted a synergistic effect of FH and the APOE ε4 allele to intensify amyloid-beta deposition and reduce glucose use in regions of the MTL and other AD-related brain regions.
source: Our findings are in line with results from a voxel-wise study in humans noting a synergistic effect of FH and the APOE ε4 allele to intensify amyloid-beta deposition and reduce glucose use in regions of the MTL and other AD-related brain regions (Yi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The collection of heritable and non-heritable changes due to FH status alter the functioning of the MTL and associated structures.
source: At the systems level, these results suggest that the collection of heritable and non-heritable changes due to FH status alter the functioning of the MTL and associated structures (Yi et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: The FH effects were only observed in participants that were ≤65 years old.
source: The fact that these effects were only observed in participants that were ≤65 years old could be due to age-related differences in the effect of FH or participation differences between younger and older FH test takers.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the age limitation of FH effects.

claim: The ≤65 years old effect is partially in line with earlier smaller and more age-specific studies of FH status and cognition demonstrating an effect of FH, but only in children and younger adults.
source: The ≤65 years old effect is partially in line with earlier smaller and more age-specific studies of FH status and cognition demonstrating an effect of FH, but only in children and younger adults (Bloss et al., 2008; Parra et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The prevalence of AD rises after age 60.
source: Since the prevalence of AD rises after age 60, it is also possible that older FH participants consenting to our study are those that have remained cognitively intact.

claim: Participants that were experiencing noticeable age- or disease-related cognitive impairment may choose not to participate.
source: Thus, participants that were experiencing noticeable age- or disease-related cognitive impairment may choose not to participate.

claim: First-degree FH results in higher risk for dementia compared to second- and third-degree FH.
source: FH risk is known to vary depending on the relationship of the diagnosed relative, and previous reports have demonstrated that first-degree FH results in higher risk for dementia compared to second- and third-degree FH (Cannon-Albright et al., 2019).

claim: It is unlikely that FH self-report error is driving the significant effect of FH on PAL.
source: These results suggest that it is unlikely that FH self-report error is driving the significant effect of FH on PAL.
